question: Which of the following is popularly known as the Father of the Green Revolution in India?
solution_text:
The correct answer is M. S. Swaminathan.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Dr. M. S. Swaminathan is popularly known as the "Father of the Green Revolution in India". (भारत में हरित क्रांति के जनक)

 

• A plant geneticist, he led the introduction of High-Yielding Variety (HYV) seeds of wheat and rice in India during the mid-1960s, in collaboration with Norman Borlaug. The Mexican dwarf wheat varieties Lerma Rojo and Sonora-64 were adapted to Indian conditions, and the semi-dwarf rice variety IR-8 followed.

 

• The Green Revolution combined HYV seeds with assured irrigation, chemical fertilisers, pesticides and mechanisation, and transformed India from a food-deficit country into a self-sufficient one. Its greatest success was in Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh, and mainly in wheat.

 

• Dr. Swaminathan received the first World Food Prize in 1987, the Ramon Magsaysay Award (1971), the Padma Vibhushan, and was posthumously conferred the Bharat Ratna in 2024.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Other revolutions in Indian agriculture: White Revolution (milk) — Verghese Kurien, Operation Flood; Blue Revolution (fish); Yellow Revolution (oilseeds); Golden Revolution (horticulture and honey); Pink Revolution (prawns and onions); Silver Revolution (eggs and poultry); Grey Revolution (fertilisers); Black Revolution (petroleum); Round Revolution (potato); Golden Fibre Revolution (jute).

 

• The National Commission on Farmers (2004), chaired by Dr. Swaminathan, recommended fixing the MSP at 50% above the weighted average cost of production (C2 + 50%).

 

NOTE

 

• Verghese Kurien (Option 1): The "Father of the White Revolution" and the architect of Operation Flood; he founded AMUL and the National Dairy Development Board (NDDB) at Anand, Gujarat.

 

• Norman Borlaug (Option 3): An American agronomist known as the "Father of the Green Revolution" worldwide, awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970 — but the Indian effort is credited to Dr. Swaminathan.

 

• C. Subramaniam (Option 4): The Union Agriculture Minister during the mid-1960s who provided the political backing for the Green Revolution; he was awarded the Bharat Ratna in 1998.

question:
Which of the following statements is correct regarding the Industrial Policy Resolution, 1956?

I. Schedule A industries were reserved exclusively for the public sector.

II. Schedule C industries were left primarily to the private sector.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Both I and II.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Both statements are correct. The Industrial Policy Resolution (IPR) of 1956 divided industries into three schedules — A, B and C. (1956 की औद्योगिक नीति — तीन अनुसूचियाँ)

 

• Schedule A listed 17 industries whose future development was to be the exclusive responsibility of the State, such as arms and ammunition, atomic energy, iron and steel, heavy machinery, aircraft, railways, shipbuilding, telecommunications, coal, mineral oils, and the generation and distribution of electricity.

 

• Schedule B listed 12 industries which were to be progressively State-owned, the State taking the initiative while private enterprise supplemented its effort — for example machine tools, aluminium and other non-ferrous metals, fertilisers, drugs, and road and sea transport.

 

• Schedule C covered all the remaining industries, whose development was left primarily to the private sector, though subject to government regulation through the licensing system under the Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The IPR 1956 is called the "Economic Constitution of India", and it formed the basis of the Second Five Year Plan (Mahalanobis model). Its aim was the establishment of a "socialistic pattern of society", giving the public sector the commanding heights of the economy.

 

• Sequence of industrial policies: 1948 (first policy statement), 1956, 1977 (emphasis on small and cottage industries, District Industries Centres), 1980, and the New Industrial Policy of 1991, which abolished licensing for most industries, cut the reserved public sector list, and ushered in LPG — Liberalisation, Privatisation and Globalisation.

 

NOTE

 

• Options 1, 2 and 4 are incorrect, because both the given statements accurately describe the classification made by the 1956 Resolution.

question: Which atmospheric layer is responsible for the reflection of radio waves, enabling long-distance radio communication?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Ionosphere.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Ionosphere reflects radio waves back to the Earth and thus makes long-distance radio communication possible. (आयनमंडल — रेडियो तरंगों का परावर्तन)

 

• It lies roughly between 80 km and 400 km above the surface and forms the lower part of the thermosphere. It contains a high concentration of free electrons and ions, produced when solar ultraviolet and X-ray radiation strips electrons from atmospheric gases — hence the name.

 

• Because these charged particles reflect radio waves, signals can be bounced between the ionosphere and the ground and so travel far beyond the horizon, despite the curvature of the Earth.

 

• The aurora borealis and aurora australis also occur in this region.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Layers of the atmosphere in order: Troposphere → Stratosphere → Mesosphere → Thermosphere (containing the Ionosphere) → Exosphere.

 

• The ionosphere is divided into the D, E and F layers; the F layer (Appleton layer) reflects the highest frequencies and is most useful for long-distance communication, while the E layer is sometimes called the Kennelly-Heaviside layer.

 

• Ionospheric reflection is affected by solar flares and geomagnetic storms, which can disrupt radio and satellite communication.

 

NOTE

 

• Mesosphere (Option 1): From about 50 km to 80 km; the coldest layer, reaching nearly -100°C at the mesopause, and the layer in which meteors burn up.

 

• Exosphere (Option 2): The outermost layer, extending into space, extremely thin, from which light gases such as hydrogen and helium escape into space.

 

• Troposphere (Option 4): The lowest layer, where all weather phenomena occur; temperature falls with height at the normal lapse rate of 6.5°C per km.

question: The ozone layer mainly absorbs which type of solar radiation?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Ultraviolet (UV) rays.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The ozone layer mainly absorbs the sun's ultraviolet (UV) radiation, particularly the harmful UV-B rays. (ओज़ोन परत — पराबैंगनी किरणों का अवशोषण)

 

• Ozone (O₃) is a triatomic form of oxygen concentrated in the stratosphere at a height of about 15 to 35 km. By absorbing UV radiation it protects life on Earth from skin cancer, cataracts, weakened immunity and damage to crops and marine phytoplankton. It is therefore called the protective umbrella or shield of the Earth.

 

• This absorption also explains why the temperature rises with height in the stratosphere.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Ozone depletion is caused mainly by chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), halons and carbon tetrachloride. The Montreal Protocol (1987) was adopted to phase out ozone-depleting substances, and 16 September is observed as the World Ozone Day. The ozone hole is largest over Antarctica.

 

• Types of UV radiation: UV-A (least harmful, mostly reaches the surface), UV-B (largely absorbed by ozone, harmful), and UV-C (most harmful, completely absorbed by ozone and oxygen).

 

• Ozone at ground level, by contrast, is a pollutant and a component of photochemical smog — hence the phrase "good up high, bad nearby".

 

NOTE

 

• Infrared rays (Option 1): These are absorbed mainly by greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide, water vapour and methane, producing the greenhouse effect — not by ozone.

 

• Gamma rays (Option 3) and X-rays (Option 4): These extremely high-energy radiations are absorbed much higher up, chiefly in the thermosphere and ionosphere, by nitrogen and oxygen atoms.

question: Which of the following structures prevents the trachea (windpipe) from collapsing during breathing?
solution_text:
The correct answer is C-shaped cartilaginous rings.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The trachea (windpipe) is supported by C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage, which keep the air passage permanently open and prevent it from collapsing when the air pressure inside falls during inhalation. (श्वासनली — C-आकार के उपास्थि वलय)

 

• There are about 16 to 20 such rings. They are incomplete at the back, where the trachea lies against the oesophagus; this gap is bridged by smooth muscle, so that the oesophagus can expand when food is swallowed.

 

• The trachea is roughly 10-12 cm long, runs from the larynx down into the chest, and divides into the right and left bronchi.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Path of air in the human respiratory system: Nostrils → Nasal cavity → Pharynx → Larynx (voice box) → Trachea → Bronchi → Bronchioles → Alveoli.

 

• Gaseous exchange takes place in the alveoli, of which there are about 300 million in the lungs, giving a surface area of some 70-80 square metres.

 

• The diaphragm and the intercostal muscles bring about breathing movements. The right lung has three lobes and the left lung two, the smaller left lung making room for the heart. The lungs are covered by a double membrane called the pleura.

 

NOTE

 

• Smooth muscles (Option 1): Present in the walls of the trachea and bronchioles and control their diameter, but they do not provide the structural support that prevents collapse.

 

• Alveoli (Option 2): Tiny air sacs at the ends of the bronchioles where exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide occurs.

 

• Epiglottis (Option 4): A flap of cartilage that covers the opening of the larynx during swallowing, so that food enters the oesophagus and not the windpipe.

question: Which of the following coins was introduced by Iltutmish during the Delhi Sultanate?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Tanka.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Iltutmish (1211-1236) introduced the silver Tanka and the copper Jital, and these became the basis of the coinage of the Delhi Sultanate. (टंका — इल्तुतमिश द्वारा प्रवर्तित चाँदी का सिक्का)

 

• The silver tanka weighed about 175 grains (roughly 11 grams). Iltutmish was the first Sultan to issue a purely Arabic coinage and the first to mention the mint name on his coins.

 

• Iltutmish belonged to the Slave (Mamluk) dynasty and is regarded as the real consolidator of the Delhi Sultanate. He shifted the capital from Lahore to Delhi, organised the Iqta system, created the Turkan-i-Chihalgani (Corps of Forty), obtained a letter of investiture (Mansur) from the Caliph of Baghdad in 1229, and completed the Qutub Minar.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Iltutmish nominated his daughter Razia Sultan as his successor — she became the first and only woman ruler of the Delhi Sultanate.

 

• Coins of medieval India frequently asked in SSC: Muhammad bin Tughlaq introduced token currency of bronze and copper (1329-30); Sher Shah Suri introduced the silver Rupiya and the copper Dam; the Gupta gold coins were called Dinaras.

 

NOTE

 

• Dinara (Option 1): The gold coin of the Gupta period, so named after the Roman denarius; the Guptas issued the largest number of gold coins in ancient India.

 

• Rupiya (Option 3): The silver coin introduced by Sher Shah Suri (1540-45), weighing about 178 grains — the ancestor of the modern rupee.

 

• Dam (Option 4): The copper coin of Sher Shah Suri, later continued under the Mughals.

question: Pataliputra became the capital of Magadha during the reign of:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Udayin.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Pataliputra became the capital of Magadha during the reign of Udayin (Udayabhadra), the son and successor of Ajatashatru, in about the 5th century BCE. (उदयिन — पाटलिपुत्र को राजधानी बनाया)

 

• Udayin shifted the capital from Rajgir (Girivraja) to Pataliputra, which he founded at the confluence of the Ganga and the Son. The site was chosen for its strategic strength — protected by rivers on several sides, it was called a water fort (Jaladurga) — and for its command over river trade.

 

• Pataliputra remained the capital under the Shishunagas, Nandas, Mauryas and later the Guptas, and is identified with modern Patna in Bihar.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Ajatashatru is said to have first built a fort at Pataligrama against the Lichchhavis, and Udayin developed it into the capital city.

 

• Dynasties of Magadha in order: Haryanka → Shishunaga → Nanda → Maurya → Shunga → Kanva.

 

• The rise of Magadha was aided by fertile alluvial soil, the iron ore of the Chhotanagpur region, the strategic location of Rajgir among five hills and of Pataliputra at a river confluence, and the use of elephants in warfare.

 

NOTE

 

• Bimbisara (Option 1): The founder of the Haryanka dynasty, whose capital was Rajgir (Girivraja); he followed a policy of matrimonial alliances and annexed Anga.

 

• Ajatashatru (Option 3): Son of Bimbisara; he defeated the Lichchhavis using the Rathamusala and Mahashilakantaka, and convened the First Buddhist Council at Rajgir.

 

• Mahapadma Nanda (Option 4): Founder of the Nanda dynasty, called Ekarat and Sarvakshatrantaka; he ruled from Pataliputra, but it was already the capital by then.

question: Megasthenes, the Greek ambassador in the court of Chandragupta Maurya, wrote:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Indica.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Megasthenes wrote "Indica", an account of India based on his stay at the court of Chandragupta Maurya at Pataliputra. (इंडिका — मेगस्थनीज)

 

• He came as the ambassador of Seleucus Nicator after the treaty of about 303 BCE. The original work is lost, and it survives only in fragments quoted by later Greek and Roman writers such as Strabo, Arrian, Diodorus and Pliny.

 

• Indica describes the city of Pataliputra, its wooden fortifications and administration by a committee of thirty divided into six boards, the seven castes into which he wrongly divided Indian society, the military administration, and the absence of slavery and of famine — statements that historians treat with caution.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Other foreign accounts for SSC: Fa-Hien (Chinese, during Chandragupta II), Hiuen Tsang (during Harshavardhana, wrote *Si-Yu-Ki*), I-tsing, Al-Biruni (*Kitab-ul-Hind*, came with Mahmud of Ghazni), Ibn Battuta (*Rehla*, during Muhammad bin Tughlaq), Marco Polo, Nicolo Conti, Abdur Razzaq and Domingo Paes (Vijayanagara).

 

NOTE

 

• Arthashastra (Option 1): Written by Kautilya (Chanakya/Vishnugupta), the minister of Chandragupta Maurya; it is a treatise on statecraft, economics and administration, rediscovered by R. Shamasastry in 1905.

 

• Rajatarangini (Option 2): Written by Kalhana in the 12th century; it is a chronicle of the kings of Kashmir and is regarded as the first work of Indian history in the modern sense.

 

• Harshacharita (Option 4): Written by Banabhatta, the court poet of Harshavardhana; Bana also wrote Kadambari.

question: Khoria is a famous folk dance of which Indian state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Haryana.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Khoria is a famous folk dance of Haryana, performed by women. (खोरिया — हरियाणा का लोक नृत्य)

 

• It is performed mainly on festive and marriage occasions, especially by the women of the bridegroom's family before the wedding procession sets out. The songs are humorous and satirical, and the dancers often mimic everyday village activities.

 

• Khoria is closely related to the Ghoomar of Haryana and is performed in traditional dress with daman, kurti and chunder.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Other folk dances of Haryana: Dhamal (one of the oldest, performed by men on moonlit nights), Phag (Phaag), Ras Leela, Loor, Gugga, Chaupaiya, Manjira and Jhumar.

 

• Haryana was carved out of Punjab on 1 November 1966 on the recommendation of the Sardar Hukam Singh Committee (Shah Commission). Its capital, Chandigarh, is shared with Punjab and is a Union Territory.

 

NOTE

 

• Punjab (Option 2): Known for Bhangra (men) and Giddha (women), as well as Jhumar, Sammi, Luddi, Kikli and Malwai Giddha.

 

• Rajasthan (Option 3): Known for Ghoomar, Kalbelia (UNESCO-listed), Kachhi Ghodi, Chari, Terah Taali, Bhavai and Gair.

 

• Himachal Pradesh (Option 4): Known for Nati (which holds a Guinness record as the largest folk dance), Kinnauri Nati, Losar Shona Chuksam and Dangi.

question: Which of the following folk dances is traditionally performed during the Navratri festival in Gujarat?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Garba.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Garba is the folk dance traditionally performed during the Navratri festival in Gujarat, in honour of the Goddess Amba (Shakti). (गरबा — गुजरात, नवरात्रि)

 

• Dancers move in concentric circles around a centrally placed earthen pot with holes, lit with a lamp inside, called the Garbo or Garbha Deep, which symbolises the womb and the divine energy of creation. The word itself derives from the Sanskrit garbha meaning 'womb'.

 

• Garba of Gujarat was inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2023, becoming India's fifteenth entry on the list.

 

• Dandiya Raas, performed with a pair of decorated sticks, is the related dance performed after the aarti and depicts the mock-fight between the Goddess and the demon Mahishasura.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Other folk dances of Gujarat: Tippani, Padhar, Hudo, Bhavai, Timli and Siddi Dhamal.

 

• India's UNESCO intangible heritage entries also include Kutiyattam, Vedic chanting, Ramlila, Ramman, Chhau dance, Kalbelia, Buddhist chanting of Ladakh, Sankirtana of Manipur, Yoga, Kumbh Mela and Durga Puja of Kolkata.

 

NOTE

 

• Bhangra (Option 1): A vigorous harvest dance of Punjab, associated with Baisakhi.

 

• Ghoomar (Option 2): A graceful dance of Rajasthan, performed by women in swirling ghagras, originally by the Bhil community.

 

• Bihu (Option 4): The most famous folk dance of Assam, associated with the Bihu festival marking the Assamese New Year and the harvest.

question: Which type of meristematic tissue is responsible for the secondary growth (increase in girth) of stems and roots?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Lateral meristem.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The lateral meristem is responsible for secondary growth, that is, the increase in the girth (thickness) of stems and roots. (पार्श्व विभज्योतक — तने और जड़ की मोटाई में वृद्धि)

 

• It lies along the sides of the plant axis and is also called the cambium. Its two forms are the vascular cambium, which produces secondary xylem inwards and secondary phloem outwards, and the cork cambium (phellogen), which produces the protective cork.

 

• This activity is responsible for the formation of annual rings in the wood of trees, by which the age of a tree can be determined — the study known as dendrochronology.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Meristematic tissue consists of actively dividing cells that are small, thin-walled, densely cytoplasmic, with large nuclei and no vacuoles or intercellular spaces.

 

• Types of meristem by position:
◦ Apical meristem — at the tips of roots and shoots; causes primary growth, that is, increase in length.
◦ Intercalary meristem — at the base of leaves or internodes; helps in the regrowth of grasses after grazing or mowing.
◦ Lateral meristem — along the sides; causes secondary growth.

 

• Permanent tissues are formed when meristematic cells lose the power of division and become specialised — simple (parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma) and complex (xylem and phloem).

 

NOTE

 

• Apical meristem (Option 1): Increases the length of the plant, not its girth.

 

• Intercalary meristem (Option 2): Also contributes to elongation, particularly in monocots such as grasses.

 

• Permanent meristem (Option 4): Not a valid category — 'permanent' and 'meristematic' are the two opposite classes of plant tissue, so the term is self-contradictory.

question: Which of the following plants shows rapid regrowth after grazing due to the presence of intercalary meristem?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Grass.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Grass shows rapid regrowth after grazing or mowing because of the presence of the intercalary meristem. (अंतर्विष्ट विभज्योतक — घास की तेज़ी से पुनर्वृद्धि)

 

• The intercalary meristem lies at the base of the leaves and internodes, that is, below the region that is grazed or cut. Since the dividing cells are not removed by the grazing animal or the lawnmower, the plant is able to grow again quickly from that point.

 

• This is why lawns and pasture grasses recover swiftly, and it is an important adaptation of monocots, especially the grass family (Poaceae), which includes wheat, rice, maize, sugarcane and bamboo.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• In most dicot trees, growth in length occurs at the apical meristem situated at the tips of shoots. If the tip is browsed off, growth from that point stops and the plant must branch out instead — a much slower process.

 

• Removing the apical bud releases the lateral buds from apical dominance, which is why gardeners prune or pinch plants to make them bushier.

 

• Bamboo, which also possesses intercalary meristem, is among the fastest-growing plants in the world.

 

NOTE

 

• Mango (Option 1), Neem (Option 2) and Banyan (Option 4): All are dicot trees with woody stems. They grow in length through the apical meristem and in girth through the lateral meristem (cambium), and lack the intercalary meristem that allows rapid regrowth after grazing.

question: Nanda Devi Raj Jat Yatra, one of the longest religious pilgrimages in India, is associated with which Indian state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Uttarakhand.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Nanda Devi Raj Jat Yatra is associated with Uttarakhand and is one of the longest religious pilgrimages in India. (नंदा देवी राज जात यात्रा — उत्तराखंड)

 

• It is held once in about twelve years and covers roughly 280 km on foot over about three weeks, through the Chamoli district of the Garhwal Himalaya, ending at Homkund near the base of Trishul.

 

• The yatra is dedicated to Goddess Nanda Devi, regarded as the presiding deity of the region and, in local belief, a daughter of the hills being escorted to her husband's home in Kailash. A four-horned ram (chausingya khadu) is believed to lead the procession.

 

• It is often called the "Himalayan Kumbh" because of its scale and the interval between its celebrations.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Nanda Devi (7,816 m) is the highest mountain entirely within India and the second highest peak in India after Kangchenjunga. The Nanda Devi Biosphere Reserve and the Valley of Flowers National Park together form a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

 

• Other festivals of Uttarakhand: Kumbh Mela at Haridwar, Kanwar Yatra, Harela, Ganga Dussehra, Uttarayani and Bikhauti. The Char Dham — Badrinath, Kedarnath, Gangotri and Yamunotri — are also in this state.

 

NOTE

 

• Himachal Pradesh (Option 1): Known for the Kullu Dussehra, Minjar Fair (Chamba), Lavi Fair (Rampur) and Losar.

 

• Sikkim (Option 3): Known for Losar, Saga Dawa, Pang Lhabsol and the Bumchu festival.

 

• Arunachal Pradesh (Option 4): Known for Losar, Solung, Mopin, Dree and Nyokum.

question: Thrissur Pooram, one of the most famous temple festivals of India, is celebrated in:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Kerala.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Thrissur Pooram is celebrated in Thrissur, Kerala, and is regarded as the most spectacular temple festival of India. (त्रिशूर पूरम — केरल)

 

• It is held in the Malayalam month of Medam (April-May), on the day when the Pooram star coincides with the full moon, at the Vadakkunnathan Temple, dedicated to Lord Shiva.

 

• The festival was begun in the late 18th century by Raja Rama Varma, known as Sakthan Thampuran, the ruler of Cochin. Its chief attractions are the procession of gorgeously caparisoned elephants, the Kudamattam — the ceremonial exchange of brightly coloured parasols — the Panchavadyam and Melam percussion ensembles, and a grand fireworks display (Vedikettu).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Other festivals of Kerala: Onam (the state festival, associated with King Mahabali, and marked by Vallamkali snake-boat races and the Pulikali tiger dance), Vishu, Theyyam and the Nehru Trophy Boat Race at Punnamada Lake, Alappuzha.

 

• Kerala's classical arts include Kathakali, Mohiniyattam and Koodiyattam, the last being India's first entry on the UNESCO intangible heritage list (2001).

 

NOTE

 

• Tamil Nadu (Option 1): Known for Pongal, the Chithirai Festival at Madurai, Natyanjali at Chidambaram and the Mahamaham at Kumbakonam.

 

• Karnataka (Option 3): Known for the Mysuru Dasara, the Hampi Utsav and Ugadi.

 

• Odisha (Option 4): Known for the Rath Yatra of Puri, Konark Dance Festival, Raja Parba and Bali Jatra.

question: Which of the following is the classical dance of Andhra Pradesh?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Kuchipudi.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Kuchipudi is the classical dance of Andhra Pradesh. (कुचिपुड़ी — आंध्र प्रदेश)

 

• It takes its name from the village of Kuchelapuram (Kuchipudi) in the Krishna district. It was systematised in the 17th century by Siddhendra Yogi, whose dance-drama "Bhama Kalapam", based on the story of Satyabhama, remains its best-known composition.

 

• Its distinctive features include a combination of dance, song and acting (the performer often speaks and sings), quicksilver footwork, and the famous Tarangam, in which the dancer performs balanced on the rim of a brass plate, sometimes with a pot of water on the head.

 

• The accompanying music is Carnatic, with the mridangam, violin, flute and cymbals; the traditional text underlying all classical dance is Bharata's Natyashastra.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The eight classical dances of India recognised by the Sangeet Natak Akademi:
◦ Bharatanatyam — Tamil Nadu
◦ Kathak — Uttar Pradesh / North India
◦ Kathakali — Kerala
◦ Mohiniyattam — Kerala
◦ Kuchipudi — Andhra Pradesh
◦ Odissi — Odisha
◦ Manipuri — Manipur
◦ Sattriya — Assam (recognised in 2000)

 

• Folk forms of Andhra Pradesh include Burrakatha, Veeranatyam, Dhimsa and Butta Bommalu.

 

NOTE

 

• Kathakali (Option 1) and Mohiniyattam (Option 2): Both belong to Kerala — Kathakali is a vigorous, male-dominated dance-drama with elaborate make-up (Chutti) and costumes, while Mohiniyattam is a graceful solo dance performed by women in white and gold.

 

• Manipuri (Option 4): Belongs to Manipur; it is devotional and gentle, centred on the Ras Leela of Radha and Krishna, and includes the vigorous male Pung Cholom and Thang-Ta.

question: Why does sweating help in cooling the human body?
option_2: Sweat reflects heat from the body.
option_3: Evaporation of sweat absorbs latent heat from the body.
option_4: Sweat prevents heat from leaving the body.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Evaporation of sweat absorbs latent heat from the body.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Sweating cools the body because the evaporation of sweat absorbs latent heat from the surface of the skin. (पसीने के वाष्पन से गुप्त ऊष्मा का अवशोषण)

 

• To change from the liquid to the vapour state, water requires energy known as the latent heat of vaporisation — about 22.5 × 10⁵ J/kg (540 cal/g) for water. This energy is drawn from the body, and the skin is therefore cooled.

 

• Evaporation is a surface phenomenon that occurs at all temperatures; it is faster when the temperature is high, the humidity is low, the surface area is large and the wind speed is high.

 

• This is also why sweating gives little relief on a humid day — the air is already nearly saturated, so evaporation is slow.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The same principle explains why water stays cool in an earthen pot (matka) — water seeps through the pores and evaporates, cooling the rest; why we feel cold when spirit or petrol is spilt on the palm; why desert coolers work; and why people sprinkle water on rooftops on hot evenings.

 

• The regulation of body temperature is controlled by the hypothalamus, and the normal human body temperature is about 37°C (98.6°F).

 

NOTE

 

• Option 1 is factually wrong; sweating lowers body temperature rather than raising it.

 

• Option 2 is incorrect, because a thin film of sweat does not act as a reflector of heat; the cooling is caused by evaporation, not reflection.

 

• Option 4 reverses the process — if sweat prevented heat from leaving the body it would cause overheating, not cooling.

question: Which of the following language families does Tamil belong to?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Dravidian.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Tamil belongs to the Dravidian family of languages. (तमिल — द्रविड़ भाषा परिवार)

 

• The Dravidian family is spoken chiefly in South India by about 20% of the Indian population. Its four major literary languages are Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam; Telugu has the largest number of speakers among them.

 

• Tamil is the oldest living Dravidian language and was the first language to be declared a Classical Language of India, in 2004. Its earliest literature is the Sangam corpus, and the Tolkappiyam is its oldest surviving grammar.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Language families of India:
◦ Indo-Aryan (Indo-European) — the largest, spoken by about 78% of Indians: Hindi, Bengali, Marathi, Gujarati, Punjabi, Odia, Assamese, Urdu, Sanskrit.
◦ Dravidian — about 20%: Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam, Tulu, Gondi, Brahui.
◦ Austro-Asiatic (Austric) — about 1.2%: Santhali, Mundari, Ho, Khasi.
◦ Tibeto-Burman (Sino-Tibetan) — about 0.6%: Manipuri (Meitei), Bodo, Naga languages, Ladakhi.

 

• The Eighth Schedule of the Constitution currently lists 22 languages. The Classical Languages of India are Tamil (2004), Sanskrit (2005), Telugu and Kannada (2008), Malayalam (2013), Odia (2014) and, added in 2024, Marathi, Pali, Prakrit, Assamese and Bengali.

 

NOTE

 

• Indo-European (Option 1): Includes the Indo-Aryan languages of northern India, not Tamil.

 

• Austro-Asiatic (Option 3): Includes the Munda languages of central and eastern India and Khasi of Meghalaya.

 

• Tibeto-Burman (Option 4): Includes the languages of the Himalayan and North-Eastern regions.

question:
Which of the following statements is correct regarding modern safety matches?

I. Red phosphorus is coated on the striking surface of the matchbox.

II. White phosphorus is used on the striking surface of modern safety matches.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Neither I nor II.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• As framed in this question, neither statement is accepted as correct.

 

• Statement II is clearly wrong. White phosphorus is never used in modern safety matches. It is highly toxic, spontaneously inflammable in air, and caused the industrial disease known as "phossy jaw" among match workers; its use in matches was banned by international agreement. Modern safety matches use red phosphorus, which is non-toxic and far more stable.

 

• Statement I is rejected here because of the way the composition is described: the striking surface of a modern safety matchbox contains a mixture of red phosphorus with powdered glass and a binder — red phosphorus is not simply *coated* on it by itself, and the match head carries the oxidising agent potassium chlorate with antimony trisulphide and sulphur. (सुरक्षा दियासलाई — रगड़ने वाली सतह पर लाल फॉस्फोरस का मिश्रण)

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• How a safety match works: friction converts a little of the red phosphorus into white phosphorus, which ignites instantly; this sets off the potassium chlorate in the head, which supplies oxygen, and the antimony trisulphide and sulphur then burn. Because the two reactants are kept separate — one on the box and one on the head — the match cannot light on any other surface, which is why it is called a safety match.

 

• Allotropes of phosphorus: White (yellow) — highly reactive, poisonous, stored under water, glows in the dark (chemiluminescence); Red — polymeric, stable, non-poisonous, used in matches; Black — the most stable form, and a conductor of electricity.

 

NOTE

 

• Options 1, 2 and 3 are incorrect, since white phosphorus is definitely not used in modern safety matches and the description in statement I does not correctly represent the composition of the striking surface.

question: Which of the following is a qualitative instrument of the Reserve Bank of India's monetary policy?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Moral Suasion.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Moral Suasion is a qualitative (selective) instrument of the Reserve Bank's monetary policy. (नैतिक दबाव — गुणात्मक उपकरण)

 

• It refers to the RBI's use of persuasion, advice, requests and informal pressure — through letters, speeches, meetings and discussions with bankers — to influence the lending behaviour of commercial banks. It carries no legal compulsion and works through moral and professional influence.

 

• Quantitative instruments control the total volume of credit in the economy and affect all sectors alike; qualitative instruments control the direction and use of credit, channelling it towards priority sectors and away from speculative ones.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Quantitative (general) instruments: Bank Rate, Repo Rate and Reverse Repo Rate, Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR), Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR), Open Market Operations (OMO), Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) and the Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF).

 

• Qualitative (selective) instruments: Moral Suasion, Margin Requirements, Credit Rationing, Consumer Credit Regulation, Direct Action and Publicity.

 

• Monetary policy is decided by the six-member Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), chaired by the RBI Governor, with three members from the RBI and three appointed by the Government; the Governor has a casting vote. The current inflation target is 4%, with a tolerance band of ±2%.

 

NOTE

 

• Cash Reserve Ratio (Option 1): The proportion of a bank's net demand and time liabilities that must be kept as cash reserves with the RBI — a quantitative tool, on which no interest is paid.

 

• Open Market Operations (Option 2): The purchase and sale of government securities by the RBI to inject or absorb liquidity — a quantitative tool.

 

• Repo Rate (Option 4): The rate at which the RBI lends short-term funds to commercial banks against government securities — the principal quantitative policy rate.

question: Which of the following cities is NOT home to an official Government of India mint?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Chennai.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Chennai does NOT have a Government of India mint. India has four mints, located at Mumbai, Kolkata, Hyderabad and Noida. (भारत की चार टकसालें — मुंबई, कोलकाता, हैदराबाद, नोएडा)

 

• The mints are operated by the Security Printing and Minting Corporation of India Limited (SPMCIL), a public sector undertaking under the Ministry of Finance, established in 2006.

 

• Coins are minted and issued by the Government of India under the Coinage Act, 2011, and are put into circulation through the Reserve Bank of India. Each mint places a distinctive mint mark below the year on the coin — a diamond for Mumbai, no mark for Kolkata, a star for Hyderabad and a solid dot for Noida.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Currency note presses: Nashik (Maharashtra) and Dewas (Madhya Pradesh) under SPMCIL, and Mysuru (Karnataka) and Salboni (West Bengal) under BRBNMPL, a wholly owned subsidiary of the RBI.

 

• Security paper is manufactured at the Security Paper Mill, Hoshangabad, and the Bank Note Paper Mill at Mysuru. The India Security Press and the Currency Note Press are both at Nashik.

 

• The one-rupee note is issued by the Government of India and bears the signature of the Finance Secretary; all other notes are issued by the RBI and bear the Governor's signature.

 

NOTE

 

• Mumbai (Option 1): The oldest mint, established in 1829; mint mark — diamond.

 

• Hyderabad (Option 2): Established in 1903 by the Nizam and taken over by the Government of India in 1950; mint mark — star.

 

• Kolkata (Option 3): Established in 1757 (Alipore mint, 1829); it uses no mint mark.

question: Mangampet, one of the world's largest deposits of barytes, is located in which Indian state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Andhra Pradesh.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Mangampet, in the Kadapa (Cuddapah) district of Andhra Pradesh, holds one of the largest single deposits of barytes in the world. (मंगमपेट — आंध्र प्रदेश)

 

• Barytes (barite) is barium sulphate (BaSO₄), a heavy, non-metallic mineral. Its chief use is as a weighting agent in drilling muds for oil and natural gas wells, which accounts for the bulk of world demand; it is also used in paints, rubber, paper, glass and in barium meals for X-ray examination of the digestive tract.

 

• India is among the leading producers of barytes in the world, and Andhra Pradesh accounts for almost the entire Indian production. The Mangampet mine is operated by the Andhra Pradesh Mineral Development Corporation (APMDC).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Mineral-state pairs frequently asked in SSC: Mica — Jharkhand, Bihar, Andhra Pradesh, Rajasthan (Koderma is the largest mica-producing area); Copper — Khetri (Rajasthan), Singhbhum (Jharkhand), Balaghat (Madhya Pradesh); Gold — Kolar and Hutti (Karnataka); Manganese — Odisha, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra; Bauxite — Odisha (Kalahandi, Koraput); Iron ore — Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka, Jharkhand; Diamond — Panna (Madhya Pradesh); Uranium — Jaduguda (Jharkhand).

 

• The Kadapa (Cuddapah) system of rocks is also known for its rich deposits of asbestos, limestone and barytes.

 

NOTE

 

• Odisha (Option 2): Leads in iron ore, bauxite, chromite and manganese, but not in barytes.

 

• Karnataka (Option 3): Known for gold (Kolar, Hutti) and iron ore (Bellary, Kudremukh).

 

• Chhattisgarh (Option 4): Known for iron ore (Bailadila, Dalli-Rajhara), coal (Korba) and tin ore, the only significant tin-producing state.

question: Who is the author of the famous novel "The Guide"?
solution_text:
The correct answer is R. K. Narayan.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "The Guide" was written by R. K. Narayan and published in 1958. (द गाइड — आर. के. नारायण)

 

• It won him the Sahitya Akademi Award in 1960, and remains his best-known work. It tells the story of Raju, a tourist guide who becomes, almost by accident, a spiritual guide and finally a reluctant holy man undertaking a fast for rain. It was made into a celebrated Hindi film in 1965 starring Dev Anand and Waheeda Rehman.

 

• Most of Narayan's fiction is set in the imaginary South Indian town of Malgudi, which he created in his first novel "Swami and Friends" (1935).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Other works by R. K. Narayan: *The Bachelor of Arts*, *The Dark Room*, *The English Teacher*, *The Financial Expert*, *Mr Sampath*, *The Man-Eater of Malgudi*, *The Vendor of Sweets*, *Malgudi Days* and *A Tiger for Malgudi*.

 

• He was awarded the Padma Bhushan (1964) and the Padma Vibhushan (2000), and was nominated to the Rajya Sabha. Along with Mulk Raj Anand and Raja Rao, he is regarded as one of the "Big Three" of early Indian writing in English.

 

NOTE

 

• Mulk Raj Anand (Option 2): Author of Untouchable, *Coolie*, *Two Leaves and a Bud* and *The Big Heart*, known for his social realism.

 

• Raja Rao (Option 3): Author of Kanthapura, *The Serpent and the Rope* (Sahitya Akademi Award) and *The Cat and Shakespeare*.

 

• Ruskin Bond (Option 4): Author of *The Room on the Roof*, *The Blue Umbrella*, *A Flight of Pigeons* and *Our Trees Still Grow in Dehra*.

question: The Tomb of Sheikh Salim Chishti is located at:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Fatehpur Sikri.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Tomb of Sheikh Salim Chishti stands at Fatehpur Sikri, near Agra in Uttar Pradesh, within the courtyard of the Jama Masjid. (शेख सलीम चिश्ती का मकबरा — फतेहपुर सीकरी)

 

• It was built by Akbar in about 1580-81 and later refaced in white marble. It is famous for its exquisitely carved jali (lattice) screens and serpentine brackets, and is one of the finest examples of marble work in Mughal architecture.

 

• Sheikh Salim Chishti was a Sufi saint of the Chishti order whose blessing Akbar sought for the birth of an heir. When Prince Salim — later Jahangir — was born in 1569, Akbar named him after the saint and built his new capital Fatehpur Sikri at that very place.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Fatehpur Sikri, founded in 1571 and abandoned around 1585 reportedly for want of water, was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986. It also contains the Buland Darwaza — at about 54 m the highest gateway in the world, built to commemorate the conquest of Gujarat — the Panch Mahal, Diwan-i-Khas, Jodha Bai's Palace and the Ibadat Khana.

 

• The Chishti order was introduced in India by Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti, whose dargah is at Ajmer; other saints of the order include Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki, Baba Farid, Nizamuddin Auliya and Nasiruddin Chirag-i-Dehlvi.

 

NOTE

 

• Agra Fort (Option 1): Built by Akbar in 1565 in red sandstone; it contains the Jahangiri Mahal, Khas Mahal, Moti Masjid and the Musamman Burj.

 

• Humayun's Tomb (Option 2): Built at Delhi in 1570 by Hamida Banu Begum; designed by the Persian architect Mirak Mirza Ghiyas, it is called the precursor of the Taj Mahal.

 

• Sikandra (Option 4): Near Agra; the site of Akbar's own tomb, begun by him and completed by Jahangir.

question: Which of the following bacteria lives in the root nodules of leguminous plants and fixes atmospheric nitrogen?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Rhizobium.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Rhizobium is the bacterium that lives in the root nodules of leguminous plants and fixes atmospheric nitrogen. (राइजोबियम — लेग्यूम पौधों की जड़ ग्रंथिकाओं में)

 

• The relationship is one of symbiosis (mutualism): the bacterium converts atmospheric nitrogen (N₂) into ammonia, which the plant can use, while the plant supplies the bacterium with food and shelter. The enzyme responsible is nitrogenase, and the pink pigment leghaemoglobin in the nodules protects it from oxygen.

 

• Leguminous plants include gram, pea, beans, groundnut, soyabean, lentil, arhar and moong. This is why farmers practise crop rotation with pulses — it restores nitrogen to the soil naturally and reduces the need for fertilisers.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Nitrogen fixation also occurs through free-living bacteria such as Azotobacter and Clostridium, through cyanobacteria (blue-green algae) such as Nostoc and Anabaena — the latter living in the water fern Azolla, used as a biofertiliser in rice fields — and through lightning, which converts nitrogen into oxides.

 

• Stages of the nitrogen cycle: **Nitrogen fixation → Nitrification (ammonia to nitrite by *Nitrosomonas*, and nitrite to nitrate by *Nitrobacter*) → Assimilation → Ammonification → Denitrification (by *Pseudomonas*, returning nitrogen to the atmosphere).**

 

• Nitrogen forms about 78% of the atmosphere and is an essential constituent of proteins, nucleic acids, chlorophyll and vitamins.

 

NOTE

 

• Azospirillum (Option 1): A free-living (associative) nitrogen-fixing bacterium found in the rhizosphere of cereals such as maize and sorghum; it does not form root nodules.

 

• Nitrosomonas (Option 2): Converts ammonia into nitrites during nitrification; it does not fix atmospheric nitrogen.

 

• Lactobacillus (Option 4): Converts milk into curd by producing lactic acid; it has no role in nitrogen fixation.

question: Which of the following is the classical dance of Odisha?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Odissi.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Odissi is the classical dance of Odisha. (ओडिसी — ओडिशा)

 

• It is regarded as one of the oldest surviving dance forms of India, its earliest evidence being the sculptures of the Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves and the dance figures of the Konark Sun Temple and the Jagannath Temple at Puri. It was performed in temples by the Maharis (devadasis) and later by boys called Gotipuas.

 

• Its distinguishing features are the two basic postures — the Tribhanga, in which the body is bent at three points (head, torso and knees), and the square Chauka stance representing Lord Jagannath — together with fluid torso movements known as Bhangas.

 

• Its themes are largely drawn from the Gita Govinda of Jayadeva, and it is closely associated with the worship of Lord Jagannath. Famous exponents include Kelucharan Mohapatra, Sonal Mansingh and Sanjukta Panigrahi.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The eight classical dances of India: Bharatanatyam (Tamil Nadu), Kathak (North India), Kathakali and Mohiniyattam (Kerala), Kuchipudi (Andhra Pradesh), Odissi (Odisha), Manipuri (Manipur) and Sattriya (Assam).

 

• Folk dances of Odisha include Chhau (Mayurbhanj), Ghumura, Ranapa, Danda Nata, Sambalpuri and Dalkhai.

 

NOTE

 

• Kuchipudi (Option 1): The classical dance of Andhra Pradesh, systematised by Siddhendra Yogi, known for the Tarangam performed on a brass plate.

 

• Bharatanatyam (Option 2): The classical dance of Tamil Nadu, the oldest codified form, sometimes called the "fire dance"; Rukmini Devi Arundale and Balasaraswati were its leading exponents.

 

• Mohiniyattam (Option 4): The graceful solo dance of Kerala, performed by women in white and gold, its name meaning the 'dance of the enchantress'.
